overview.body: This is an ENHANCE unit! You'll copy your Lab 1.1 code and give the player their first real decision. They pick a destination, and your program works out whether their roll gets them there. Make it to the beach and you win; fall short and you'll see how far you still have to go.

mentorQuote.quote: Before you write any if-elif-else code, think about testing. You've got three valid choices plus invalid input. That's four paths through your code, and each one can end in more than one way. I always sketch out my test cases first. If you can't test it, you can't trust it!

objectives: Start from a clean copy of Lab 1.1, with the parts 1.2 replaces deleted
Get the player's choice and act on it with if/elif/else
Decide whether the roll is enough with a nested if
Track where the player ends up and print the Final Trip Report

content.body: The player's first real decision. They pick 1, 2, or 3, and your program sets the destination and its distance. Anything else is an invalid choice, and the player stays in San Antonio.

An if/elif/else chain runs exactly one branch: the first one whose condition is true, or the else if none are. Every branch sets the same two variables, destination and distance, so the code after the chain works no matter which choice was made.

content.title: Indentation is the structure
content.body_html: The lines under each if, elif, and else are indented four more spaces than the line above them: eight spaces in all, because the chain is already inside main(). That indentation is how Python knows which lines belong to which branch. Every one of those lines ends with nothing after it; every if, elif, and else line ends with a colon.

content.body: The answer to the question the whole lab is about: did your roll get you there? If it did, you made it. If not, you see how far you still have to go.

This check only makes sense for a real destination, so it goes inside the else from CP2: an if inside another if, called a nested decision. The math is the same direction as Lab 1.1: distance first, then minus miles_rolled. Zero or less means you made it.

content.quote: Nested ifs look scary until you read the indentation like an outline. Eight spaces is inside the else. Twelve spaces is inside the if that's inside the else. If a line is at the wrong depth, it's in the wrong place, and Python will do exactly what the indentation says.
